tutor_context: Key facts: risk factors include spinal anaesthesia, opioids, anticholinergics, large fluid volumes, hernia and anorectal surgery, age and male sex; bladder scan is the diagnostic tool; catheterise when volume exceeds about 500 to 600 mL or the patient cannot void; overdistension beyond 1 litre risks detrusor injury; plan a trial of void. Misconceptions: more fluid helps; alpha blockers treat acute retention in women. Out of scope: suprapubic catheterisation and urology referral criteria.
plan: Management item on postoperative urinary retention after spinal anaesthesia in a rural hospital with no surgeon on site. The key is prompt catheterisation and a trial of void plan. Distractors: more fluid, an alpha blocker, and unnecessary deferral to the surgeon. Supported by perioperative literature and ANZCA acute pain guidance.

stem: You are a PGY2 on the general ward of a metropolitan general hospital with a busy medical ward and a registrar on site overnight. A 58-year-old woman was admitted this evening for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy on tomorrow morning's list after two episodes of biliary colic; she was seen in pre-admission clinic 3 weeks ago and cleared. While clerking her you learn that over the past fortnight she has had central chest tightness walking up the ramp from the car park, settling within minutes of rest, with no pain at rest. She has hypertension and smokes 15 cigarettes a day. Her admission ECG shows new T-wave inversion in V4 to V6 compared with the pre-admission tracing. She is currently pain free with normal observations.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Proceed as planned, because the symptoms are stable and lateral T-wave changes are non-specific.
Request an outpatient stress echocardiogram after discharge and allow the surgery to proceed in the morning.
Inform the anaesthetist and surgical registrar tonight of the new symptoms and ECG changes, send a troponin, and expect surgery to be deferred for cardiology assessment.
Start aspirin and a beta blocker tonight so that the operation can go ahead safely in the morning.

explanations.A: New exertional angina with new ECG changes represents an active cardiac condition; elective surgery in this setting carries a substantial risk of perioperative myocardial infarction and should not proceed until the condition has been assessed and managed.
explanations.B: Deferring the cardiac work-up until after the operation puts the risk in the wrong order; the surgery for uncomplicated biliary colic is elective and can wait, whereas the new ischaemic symptoms cannot.
explanations.C: This is correct. New-onset exertional chest pain with new T-wave inversion is a recognised active cardiac condition that requires evaluation before elective non-cardiac surgery. The resident's job is to communicate the finding promptly to the anaesthetist and surgical team, check a troponin and ensure she is reviewed; the decision to postpone belongs to them, but it is the expected outcome.
explanations.D: Starting a beta blocker on the night before surgery increases the risk of hypotension, stroke and death and is specifically advised against; aspirin alone does not make surgery safe in untreated active ischaemia.

learning_point: New exertional chest pain with new ECG changes found at preoperative assessment is an active cardiac condition: communicate it to the anaesthetic and surgical teams immediately, investigate, and expect elective surgery to be postponed pending cardiology review.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the same finding would mean cancelling the case on a visiting list and arranging cardiology advice by telehealth or transfer; the communication step is identical, and the resident should not feel pressure to let a visiting list proceed.

references.title: ANZCA PG07(A) Guideline on pre-anaesthesia consultation and patient preparation (2017)
references.locator: Identification and communication of conditions requiring optimisation before anaesthesia

references.title: ACC/AHA Guideline for perioperative cardiovascular management for noncardiac surgery (2024)
references.locator: Active cardiac conditions; unstable angina; perioperative beta-blocker initiation

tutor_context: Key facts: active cardiac conditions (unstable or new angina, recent MI, decompensated heart failure, significant arrhythmia, severe valvular disease) warrant deferral of elective surgery; beta blockers should not be started within a day of surgery; troponin and cardiology review precede rescheduling. Misconceptions: that pre-admission clearance is permanent, or that ECG changes without rest pain are benign. Out of scope: functional capacity scoring details.
plan: Management item on discovering new ischaemic symptoms and ECG changes on the night before elective surgery. The key is immediate communication and work-up with expected deferral. Distractors: proceed, defer investigation, or start beta blockers the night before. Supported by ANZCA PG07(A) and current perioperative cardiovascular guidelines.

stem: You are the PGY1 on the general ward of a metropolitan general hospital with a registrar on site overnight. A 29-year-old woman has been admitted the night before an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anaesthesia. She is otherwise well, takes no regular medications, has no family history of bleeding or anaesthetic problems, does not smoke, and has a normal examination with a body mass index of 24. Her last menstrual period was 5 weeks ago and she says her periods are sometimes irregular. The anaesthetist has asked you to make sure the "routine preoperative tests" are done before the morning and the nurse asks which forms to prepare.
lead_in: Which preoperative test is indicated for this patient?

options.text: Chest X-ray
Urine or serum pregnancy test
Resting 12-lead ECG
Coagulation screen

explanations.A: A chest X-ray is not indicated before elective surgery in a healthy young non-smoker with a normal examination; routine preoperative chest radiography does not change management and is listed among tests to avoid.
explanations.B: This is correct. Pregnancy testing should be offered to any woman of childbearing potential before surgery or anaesthesia where pregnancy cannot be excluded, and here a late and irregular period makes it clearly necessary; the result may alter the timing of surgery, drug choices and radiology.
explanations.C: A resting ECG is not required in an asymptomatic patient under 40 without cardiac risk factors undergoing low or intermediate risk surgery.
explanations.D: Coagulation tests are not indicated without a personal or family history of bleeding, liver disease or anticoagulant use; routine screening is unhelpful and is a Choosing Wisely target.

learning_point: Routine preoperative tests are selected by patient and procedure, not ordered as a bundle; in a healthy young woman the test that matters is a pregnancy test when pregnancy cannot be excluded.

references.title: ANZCA PG07(A) Guideline on pre-anaesthesia consultation and patient preparation (2017)
references.locator: Preoperative investigations: indications; pregnancy testing

references.title: Choosing Wisely Australia, ANZCA recommendations
references.locator: Avoid routine preoperative investigations in low-risk patients

tutor_context: Key facts: preoperative tests should be targeted; ECG for older patients or cardiac risk factors; chest X-ray only for active cardiorespiratory disease; coagulation only with bleeding history; pregnancy test for women of childbearing potential when pregnancy cannot be excluded, with consent. Misconception: a standard preoperative bundle for everyone. Out of scope: management if the test is positive.
plan: Easy recall item on targeted preoperative testing in a healthy young woman with a late period. Distractors are commonly over-ordered tests. Supported by ANZCA PG07(A) and Choosing Wisely Australia.

stem: You are the PGY1 covering the surgical ward of a metropolitan general hospital overnight; the surgical registrar is on site. A 78-year-old man is 2 days post anterior resection for rectal cancer with a pelvic drain that has been producing about 50 mL of serosanguineous fluid per shift. At 03:00 the nurse calls you: over the last 2 hours the drain has filled with 400 mL of frank blood, his heart rate is 112, blood pressure 98/58, respiratory rate 22 and he is pale and anxious. He takes aspirin, which was restarted this morning, and his haemoglobin yesterday was 102 g/L. He has one 20-gauge cannula in situ.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Clamp the drain to tamponade the bleeding and reassess the output in an hour.
Remove the drain, as it may be eroding a vessel, and apply a firm dressing over the site.
Give a litre of sodium chloride 0.9%, order one unit of red cells and review at the morning ward round.
Call the surgical registrar now, insert a second large-bore cannula, send a group and crossmatch and full blood count, and leave the drain unclamped.

explanations.A: Clamping a drain does not stop intra-abdominal bleeding; it hides the volume being lost and allows blood to collect in the pelvis. Drain output is the monitoring tool, not the source of the haemorrhage.
explanations.B: Removing the drain removes the only indicator of ongoing bleeding and does not address the bleeding vessel; a pressure dressing has no effect on pelvic haemorrhage.
explanations.C: Fluid and blood are part of the response, but a plan that waits until morning ignores a patient who is tachycardic and hypotensive with active bleeding and needs senior surgical review now, possibly a return to theatre.
explanations.D: This is correct. Fresh blood in a drain with haemodynamic instability on day 2 is postoperative haemorrhage until proven otherwise. The intern's role is to escalate immediately by calling the surgical registrar and activating the rapid response if criteria are met, secure two large-bore cannulas, send crossmatch and bloods, start fluid resuscitation, withhold the aspirin and keep the drain on free drainage so losses can be measured.

learning_point: Fresh blood in a surgical drain with tachycardia and hypotension is postoperative haemorrhage: escalate to the surgical registrar immediately, obtain large-bore access and crossmatch, resuscitate, and never clamp or remove the drain.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without a surgeon on site, the same steps apply with the GP or senior doctor on call, early activation of the retrieval service, and use of emergency O-negative blood if the patient deteriorates before crossmatched blood is available.

references.title: SA Health Recognising and Responding to Clinical Deterioration Policy and Rapid Detection and Response observation chart
references.locator: Escalation criteria and rapid response activation

references.title: ACSQHC Blood Management Standard and National Patient Blood Management Guidelines Module 1: Critical bleeding
references.locator: Assessment and management of acute haemorrhage

tutor_context: Key facts: a change in drain output from serous to frank blood, especially with tachycardia or hypotension, indicates haemorrhage; management is ABC, two large-bore cannulas, group and crossmatch, resuscitation, holding antiplatelets and anticoagulants, and urgent surgical review; drains are never clamped to manage bleeding. Misconceptions: clamping to tamponade; waiting for the haemoglobin to fall before acting. Out of scope: massive transfusion protocol details.
plan: Management item on fresh haemorrhage in a surgical drain with instability overnight. The key is immediate escalation with resuscitation preparation while leaving the drain draining. Distractors: clamp, remove, or fluid and wait. Supported by the SA Health deterioration policy and the National Patient Blood Management Guidelines.

stem: You are a PGY2 on the general ward of a metropolitan general hospital with a registrar on site overnight. A 22-year-old man is 3 days post open appendicectomy for a perforated appendix and has received intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate since surgery. Overnight he developed severe pain around the wound that the nurse describes as out of proportion to the appearance, needing repeated opioid doses. On examination at 05:00 he is confused and sweaty, temperature 39.4 degrees, heart rate 128, blood pressure 102/60. The wound edges show faint dusky erythema with a thin grey, foul-smelling discharge; the tenderness and induration extend well beyond the erythema, and you feel crepitus in the right flank. Bloods: white cell count 24 x 10^9/L, CRP 310 mg/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 150 micromol/L, lactate 4.1 mmol/L.
lead_in: Which interpretation of these findings is most accurate?

options.text: A necrotising soft tissue infection of the abdominal wall; this is a surgical emergency needing immediate surgical review for debridement alongside sepsis management.
A superficial incisional surgical site infection; the wound should be opened, swabbed and treated with oral antibiotics.
An intra-abdominal collection; a CT with percutaneous drainage will address the fever and the wound changes are incidental.
Cellulitis around the wound; intravenous flucloxacillin and marking the erythema for reassessment in 12 hours are appropriate.

explanations.A: This is correct. Pain out of proportion, rapidly progressive systemic toxicity, dusky skin, grey foul discharge, induration beyond the visible erythema, crepitus, hyponatraemia, marked leucocytosis and raised lactate together indicate necrotising fasciitis. Diagnosis is clinical, imaging must not delay surgery, and management is immediate senior surgical review for urgent debridement, sepsis resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics with clindamycin, and intensive care involvement.
explanations.B: A superficial site infection does not cause confusion, tachycardia, high lactate or crepitus; treating this as a simple wound infection would delay life-saving debridement by hours.
explanations.C: A collection is possible after a perforated appendix and may coexist, but it does not explain the wound-centred pain, crepitus and skin changes; arranging CT first would delay surgical exploration, which is the priority.
explanations.D: Cellulitis is confined to the skin without crepitus, dishwater discharge or pain beyond the erythema, and does not produce this degree of organ dysfunction; a 12-hour reassessment is far too slow.

learning_point: Pain out of proportion, rapidly progressive sepsis, dusky skin, grey discharge, crepitus and induration beyond the erythema around a surgical wound indicate necrotising soft tissue infection, a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate surgical debridement rather than imaging or antibiotics alone.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the same recognition triggers immediate phone contact with the surgeon and the retrieval service, sepsis management and antibiotics while transfer is arranged, because time to debridement determines survival.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections: clinical features, urgent surgical debridement and antibiotic therapy

references.title: ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard (2022)
references.locator: Recognition and early management of sepsis

tutor_context: Key facts: necrotising fasciitis features include pain out of proportion, rapid progression, crepitus, bullae, grey dishwater discharge, anaesthesia of overlying skin and systemic toxicity; LRINEC scoring supports but does not replace clinical judgement; management is surgical debridement within hours, broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin per Therapeutic Guidelines), resuscitation and ICU. Misconceptions: waiting for imaging; antibiotics alone. Out of scope: specific operative technique.
plan: High-difficulty interpretation item where a postoperative wound infection is actually necrotising fasciitis with subtle skin findings but marked systemic features. Distractors are the more common and more comfortable diagnoses. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic and the Sepsis Clinical Care Standard.

stem: You are the PGY1 assisting in the pre-admission clinic and theatre suite of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, where the visiting surgeon runs a monthly list. A 55-year-old woman, weight 78 kg, with no drug allergies and no history of multi-resistant organisms, is booked for an elective open repair of an umbilical hernia with mesh under general anaesthesia tomorrow. The anaesthetist asks you to chart her surgical antibiotic prophylaxis on the medication chart so the theatre nurse can prepare it, and to note when it should be given.
lead_in: What is the correct prophylactic antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Cefalexin 500 mg orally with breakfast on the morning of surgery.
Cefazolin 2 g intravenously at skin incision, then 8-hourly for 24 hours.
Cefazolin 2 g intravenously as a single dose within 60 minutes before skin incision.
Cefazolin 2 g intravenously in recovery after wound closure.

explanations.A: Oral cefalexin at breakfast gives unpredictable tissue levels at the time of incision and is not a recommended surgical prophylaxis regimen; intravenous administration timed to incision is required.
explanations.B: Giving the first dose at incision is slightly late, and continuing for 24 hours offers no additional protection for a clean procedure while increasing adverse effects and resistance; a single dose is standard, with intraoperative redosing only for prolonged surgery or major blood loss.
explanations.C: This is correct. For a clean procedure with mesh implantation, cefazolin 2 g intravenously (3 g if weight is 120 kg or more) is given as a single dose within 60 minutes before incision, usually at induction, so that tissue concentrations are adequate when the incision is made.
explanations.D: Prophylaxis given after wound closure is ineffective; the antibiotic must be present in tissues at the time of contamination.

learning_point: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis is a single intravenous dose of cefazolin 2 g given within 60 minutes before skin incision, not an oral dose, a postoperative dose or a prolonged course.
setting_note: On a visiting list the junior doctor often charts prophylaxis in advance; writing the dose, route and the instruction to give at induction on the chart, and confirming allergies and weight, prevents a missed or mistimed dose when the anaesthetist is also managing other cases.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis: principles (timing, dosing, duration); hernia repair

references.title: ACSQHC Surgical Antimicrobial Prophylaxis Clinical Care Standard (2020)
references.locator: Timing of administration; single dose; weight-based dosing

tutor_context: Key facts: cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 minutes before incision (3 g if 120 kg or more); redose intraoperatively after about 4 hours or major blood loss; no postoperative continuation for most procedures; vancomycin for MRSA colonisation or severe beta-lactam allergy requires earlier infusion. Misconceptions: oral prophylaxis, prolonged courses. Out of scope: prophylaxis choices for contaminated procedures.
plan: Recall item on timing, route and duration of surgical antibiotic prophylaxis for a clean mesh hernia repair on a rural visiting list. Distractors: oral dose, prolonged course, postoperative dose. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic and the ACSQHC Surgical Antimicrobial Prophylaxis Clinical Care Standard.
